conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It helps us pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, and anything that might be making motherhood harder than it needs to be.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. There are no right or wrong answers—just your honest experience over the past seven days. I’ll ask ten questions; most moms finish in just a few minutes. Ready to begin?

Over the last week, when you were able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how did that feel for you?

Honestly? Most of the time when something funny happens, I can still laugh, but it feels kind of… flat, like I’m going through the motions. I’ll smile or chuckle, but the joy doesn’t last. A few minutes later I’m back to feeling heavy and tired again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess I’d say “yes, but only sometimes.” I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, yet it feels kind of forced or doesn’t lift my mood the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I picked “hardly ever.” I used to get excited about little things—a coffee outing, a TV show, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels like there’s nothing to look forward to. Everything just seems like another task I probably won’t have energy for.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens pretty often. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good-enough mom or I missed some cue. Even little things, like spitting up more than usual, leave me feeling guilty and telling myself I should’ve known better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah—I’d say “yes, quite often.” My mind keeps jumping to worst-case scenarios about the baby: is she breathing, is she getting enough milk, am I missing something? I’ll suddenly feel my heart racing even when everything looks fine. I know it’s probably over-the-top, but I can’t seem to stop the worry.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

That happens sometimes—maybe once or twice this week. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s asleep and totally fine, and suddenly this wave of fear hits: like something awful is about to happen or I’m not safe. My chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I have to get up and pace or check on her again. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

I’d say “yes, most of the time.” Between feeding every couple of hours, trying to sleep in short bursts, and feeling like the house is falling apart, I keep thinking I can’t catch up. I start one chore and three more pop up, and I just feel buried. Some moments I manage to push through, but overall it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ve been going to bed feeling heavy and sad, and then my mind just keeps spinning—worrying about the baby, replaying everything I think I messed up. It takes me a long time to fall asleep, and when she wakes up I can’t drift off again. A couple nights this week I’ve just lain there crying quietly so I don’t wake anyone.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’d say “yes, most of the time.” I wake up feeling low, and that cloud just sticks around through the day. Even when nothing specific is wrong, I still feel weepy and empty, like I’m stuck under a gray sky I can’t get out from under.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

That’s been happening quite a lot—definitely more days than not. Sometimes it’s just a few quiet tears while I’m nursing, other times it turns into full-on sobbing when I’m alone in the bathroom. I feel overwhelmed and can’t seem to stop once I start.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself.

You've shared how, over the past week, laughter feels hollow and joy seems out of reach, even though you can still sometimes smile. You wake up under a <sym>heavy, gray cloud</sym> and go to bed with racing worries about being a <quote>good-enough mom</quote>, often lying awake in <sym>quiet tears</sym>. Little pleasures-coffee, a shower, a show-no longer spark excitement, and normal baby behaviours leave you swamped by <sym>self-blame</sym>. Frequent <sym>anxious racing heart</sym> and sudden waves of fear interrupt calm moments, leaving you shaky and convinced something awful is about to happen. Daily tasks feel like a <sym>drowning pile</sym> you can't climb out of, and crying episodes arrive <quote>more days than not</quote>, yet you firmly deny any wish to harm yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly chose the option equivalent to "Hardly at all" and described a complete loss of anticipatory pleasure for even small joys, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame for routine infant behaviors, indicating this occurs 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, uncontrollable worry and racing heart, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected panic episodes occurring 1-2 times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "yes, most of the time" and describes feeling overwhelmed, unable to catch up, and drowning in tasks</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to persistent sadness and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "yes, most of the time" and describes persistent low mood, weepiness, and emptiness matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying "quite a lot" and "more days than not," aligning with "Yes, quite often" rather than "most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 23/30 exceeds the 14-point threshold indicating <med>probable major postpartum depression</med>. Core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> are met: most-day <sym>depressed mood</sym> (Q8=3), marked <sym>loss of interest</sym> (Q2=3), <sym>fatigue</sym> implied by <quote>no energy</quote>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> (Q7=3), <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>/guilt (Q3=3), <sym>diminished ability to think/concentrate</sym> reflected in <quote>mind keeps spinning</quote>, and clinically significant distress. Anxiety items (Q4=3, Q5=2) suggest co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. No self-harm ideation (Q10=0) lowers acute risk but does not negate need for prompt care. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care doctor</med> within the next few days; bring this EPDS result.
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or <med>psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and discussion of <med>antidepressant</med> or <med>therapy options</med>.
3. Begin evidence-based <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal psychotherapy</med> focusing on postpartum adaptations; consider local mother-infant group programs.
4. Enlist practical support-partner, family, or postpartum doula-to cover night feeds or household tasks so you can secure 3-4 hour sleep blocks; practice <med>sleep hygiene</med> (dim lights, no screens at feedings, brief wind-down routine).
5. Plan daily 10-15 minute outdoor walk or gentle movement; sunlight and light exercise can modestly lift mood.
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory after treatment starts.
7. Keep emergency numbers handy: your provider's after-hours line, <med>Postpartum Support International</med> helpline 1-800-944-4773, and 988 (US) if distress escalates.
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms (≥2 wks):
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness “most of the time”
- Marked anhedonia (“hardly ever” looking forward to anything)
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting performance
- Anxious apprehension & panic spells with physical arousal
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulty linked to rumination
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed/drowning in daily tasks

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning, no self-harm ideation reported.

Screening significance: High endorsement of depressive and anxiety items consistent with possible major postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety disorder. No current safety concerns. Recommend formal clinical interview (EPDS / PHQ-9 / GAD-7) and follow-up with OB/MH provider.
